text.p: These are the leading stories in the Belgrade press on Friday. Reuters has not verified them and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- Yugoslav policy has received full recognition of the international community with the permanent lifting of sanctions, says Yugoslav President Zoran Lilic.
- Yugoslav goverment adopts platform for participation of a team of Yugoslav experts, headed by Kosta Mihajlovic, at the succession talks for the former Yugoslavia on October 14 and 15 in Brussels.
- Yugoslavia and Germany sign agreement on return of Yugoslav refugees during Yugoslav Interior Minister Vukasin Jokanovic's visit.
- Jokanovic meets German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and discusses Yugoslavia's integration in the international community and access to long-term financial aid and cooperation with the EU.
- Bulgaria asks the Brussels-based European transport commission to include the Sofia-Belgrade-Budapest highway as a main European corridor.
- Yugoslavia can expect foreign investments of $500 million in the first years after the lifting of sanctions, says Milutin Cirovic, chairman of the federal government economic council.
- Yugoslav Airlines JAT is waiting for permits for intercontinental flights, and will establish regular flights to Banja Luka and Sarajevo.
- U.S. Assistant Secretary of State John Kornblum arriving Friday for a new round of talks in Banja Luka, Pale and Sarajevo.
- Greek Foreign Minister Theodoros Pangalos will visit Belgrade, Zagreb and Sarjaevo from October 16 to 18, the Greek Foreign Ministry said.
- Representatives of the London Club of creditor banks will arrive in Belgrade in the course of next week, says John Eisenhammer of Lowe Bell Financial.

- The health protection insitute in Pristina confirmed a polio epidemic in Kosovo province in the Prizren area. There were 15 cases registered in the August-October period. Urgent vaccination of children under 14 proposed.
- Yugoslav National Bank Vice governor Ratko Banovic announces possible increase in the bank's reserve requirement currently at 10 percent.
